item.title: Why 'motocross' Sepang wasn't fixed - and is bruising riders
item.description: Multiple MotoGP riders have expressed concerns about the state of the Sepang International Circuit’s asphalt ahead of this weekend’s Malaysian Grand Prix.
item.dc:creator: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded:
Multiple MotoGP riders have expressed concerns about the state of the Sepang International Circuit’s asphalt ahead of this weekend’s Malaysian Grand Prix.

A track already in need of resurfacing was further damaged by this month’s replacement Formula 1 race - running as the 'Bahrain Grand Prix' in lieu of a race at the country's actual Sakhir track - to the point where it has now, according to some racers, become borderline dangerous to ride on.

Last resurfaced 10 years ago, the track was due to receive new asphalt ahead of this year’s MotoGP event, but delays to logistics caused by the geopolitical situation in the Middle East saw this work pushed back.

And the high downforce generated by F1 cars has caused considerable further degradation of the track at a number of key corners.

The unexpected arrival of F1 also saw remedial work planing the straights, in an attempt to remove bumps - which appears to have exacerbated the situation in other regards. The track is now shedding stones due to the forces generated by the bikes as they accelerate.

MotoGP had a similar issue at the second round of the 2026 season at the inaugural Brazilian Grand Prix in Goiania, where the main race on Sunday was cut in distance at the last minute as the track started to crumble during the Moto2 and Moto3 races.

And, speaking to riders after the opening day of practice on Friday, a number were less than happy that their request to resurface after testing hadn’t been accomplished given the state of the asphalt right now.

“The asphalt is, pardon my French, f**ked,” Jack Miller told the media.

“We told them it was f**ked already at the test. Turn 1 has no stones in it [within the surface], like absolutely none. Turn 4 has none. All the stones are coming out of the asphalt.

“This track cops a lot of abuse, and we asked for it [the resurfacing], but unfortunately there wasn’t enough time between then and now, or whatever, and I think with F1 coming it didn't help the situation.

"It’s definitely something that needs to be improved on before they come testing at the beginning of next year.”

Others went into even more detail about the issue of the stones coming loose, with a number of riders sporting fresh bruises from being hit.

“It’s a motocross track now,” VR46 Ducati rider Fabio Di Giannantonio said. “We need to wear a chest protector. There are a lot of rocks coming from the asphalt. I got a lot of rocks when I did the practice start behind another guy.”

Honda rider Luca Marini said he had to abort a run because a loose stone caused radiator damage to his RC213V bike.

“It's never good when they do these kinds of things on the asphalt,” Di Giannantonio added of the start-finish planing.

“For us with the bikes it’s never good, but I don’t know what we can do about it from now until tomorrow.”

“When I rode alone, it looked normal,” LCR Honda rider Johann Zarco added, “but when I’m following someone I received a piece of Tarmac on the body, and I think tomorrow for the [sprint] race, for the one who is not leading, for 19 riders [behind], it will be very tough.

“We will receive many hits on the arms and the neck. We are used to it, but it is a pity.”

item.title: Marquez quickest again, Martin done after three laps
item.description: MotoGP championship leader Marc Marquez completed a clean sweep of Friday practice at Sepang, as Jorge Martin withdrew from the afternoon session after three laps
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
MotoGP championship leader Marc Marquez completed a clean sweep of Friday practice at Sepang, as Jorge Martin withdrew from the afternoon session after three laps.

Martin, who broke his wrist in a crash last Saturday at Phillip Island but has foregone rest for now in favour of trying to keep his title chances alive, did 12 laps in the morning but had to end his day early.

"Together with the doctors, we decided all together to not continue and wait tonight and see tomorrow morning, because, at the moment, if he [Martin] wants to make the laptime, to make the time attack, it's for him difficult to manage the force," Aprilia team manager Paolo Bonora explained to MotoGP.com.

"So it's better to take no risk, absolutely, and we decided all together, together in particular with the doctors, Dr. [Angel] Charte, that we don't go forward during the session."

Q2 by virtue of a top-10 spot would have been a monumental longshot for Martin anyway, whereas for Marquez it looked a foregone conclusion - despite him crashing at the final corner in the early phase of the session.

He bounced back from this to head his Sepang-specialist brother Alex by 0.109s at the conclusion of the session, despite sacrificing the opportunity of one final run on a fresh soft rear.

Trackhouse Aprilia rider Ai Ogura had looked off for much of the day but uncharacteristically came alive when it came to single-lap attempts, moving up to third, ahead of the lead KTM of Pedro Acosta and VR46 Ducati rider Fabio Di Giannantonio.

Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia), Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM), Maverick Vinales (Tech3 KTM), Franco Morbidelli (VR46 Ducati) and the returning Joan Mir (Honda) picked up the remaining Q2 spots.

It will thus be Vinales's first Q2 appearance since Assen last year, pre-injury. He was 0.002s back from team-mate Bastianini, who crashed starting his final run late on.

While Bastianini got away with the crash in Q2 terms, the same wasn't true for Johann Zarco (LCR Honda) and Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati), both likewise tumbling during their final runs.

Zarco's rookie team-mate Diogo Moreira just stayed on the bike in a big moment at the last corner, but ran out of chances to enter the top 10.

Alex Rins was the lead Yamaha in 14th, narrowly ahead of Gresini Ducati stand-in Iker Lecuona and Pramac Yamaha's Jack Miller, who had a crash seven minutes into the session.

item.title: Injured Martin cleared to race in Malaysia after first practice
item.description: Jorge Martin is cleared to race at Sepang after completing FP1, but finding pace looks tough
item.dc:creator: Matt Beer
item.content:encoded:
Jorge Martin can continue with his bid to keep his MotoGP championship chase alive, having been passed fit to race in the Malaysian Grand Prix with a broken wrist.

But while he has cleared that first hurdle, his weekend got off to a mixed start in Friday morning practice at Sepang.

The good news was that he managed to complete the full session, covering 12 laps across multiple runs, and going back out again for the practice starts at the end of the session.

That mileage and his Aprilia team talking confidently about its strategy for Martin through the weekend immediately suggested he was expecting to pass the mandatory medical check after the session - which he duly did half an hour later.

Limiting the title fight damage looks tough, though. While Martin improved from being four seconds off the pace on his tentative first run, he was still 1.835s down and 20th fastest at the end of the session, so will need to find substantially more pace to have a shot at scoring significant points.

And the identity of the pacesetter was bad news for Martin too, with his title rival Marc Marquez's Ducati a comfortable fastest by 0.474s over Martin's Aprilia team-mate Marco Bezzecchi.

KTM's Pedro Acosta matched Bezzecchi's time in third, while Acosta's stablemates Enea Bastianini and Brad Binder used fresher tyres to go fourth and fifth at the end, just as sixth-placed Franco Morbidelli (VR46 Ducati) did.

While one of Aprilia's injured duo looks set to continue with the weekend, the other was ruled out during practice one.

Raul Fernandez pitted after four laps and was then declared unfit for the rest of the event, with his Trackhouse team boss Davide Brivio explaining that Fernandez's broken finger was at a point in the healing process where discomfort was particularly strong and the chance of further damage was too high if he crashed again.

Fernandez will return home to Spain for further treatment to assist the healing process before attempting to race in Qatar next weekend.

item.title: Crunch time for MotoGP as Qatar talks ramp up
item.description: Fresh doubts have been expressed by figures in the MotoGP paddock about whether next weekend’s Qatar Grand Prix can really go ahead
item.dc:creator: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded:
Fresh doubts have been expressed by figures in the MotoGP paddock about whether next weekend’s Qatar Grand Prix can go ahead - as a looming re-escalation of the war between the USA and Iran continues to prompt meetings between the championship’s 22 riders and the series organisers regarding safety assurances.

The MotoGP weekend is set to get underway at Lusail next Thursday, two days after the US midterm elections - but this week has seen a series of warnings issued by governments and media that US president Donald Trump will seek to resume hostilities with Iran as soon as voting is complete.

Qatar, which hosts the largest US air force base in the region only a few miles from the Lusail circuit, was struck by missile and drone attacks in March when asked the US first attacked Iran. And Houthi forces have launched strikes from Yemen increasingly close to Qatar in recent weeks, amid continued conflict with the neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

The threat of imminent escalation first prompted the MotoGP grid to assemble last week in Australia for a rare all-hands meeting, before follow-ups in Sepang, first with their team bosses and then with MotoGP CEO Carmelo Ezpeleta.

“We cannot go deeply into details,” explained VR46 Ducati racer Fabio Di Giannantonio when by The Race, “but let's say that the goal is to work with MotoGP to try to have the best safety, the best guarantees, insurances, for sure for all the members of the paddock, to do our job in a better way.

“I think it's fair to try to help MotoGP and Dorna to improve our sport - not only on track, also outside and also in these kinds of things. So it's not at all a fight, let's say, what we are doing is completely a cooperation to try to improve everybody's conditions to try to race there.”

However, any sort of guarantee of the 2,000-strong paddock’s safety is likely to be beyond the reach of the championship’s organisers right now, should a regional escalation cause airports in Qatar and its neighbours Saudi Arabia and the UAE to be shut down, potentially leaving the paddock trapped in an active warzone until such time as things once again cool down.

That’s backed up by increasingly severe government warnings in recent days, with a number of countries escalating their risk level for Qatar and warning that citizens should only travel there for essential reasons - as well as have a concrete escape plan for evacuation.

For the first time on Thursday in Sepang, there were even hints of teams refusing to take part in the race, with Alex Rins seeming to confirm speculation that the Japanese government’s travel advisory would prevent the country's two factory teams - Honda and Yamaha - from travelling there.

“Right now Yamaha, I think, is one of the unique ones that they don't know if they will go to Qatar,” he explained.

“I would like to talk [more] about it, but I can't. The only thing that I can say is we are really united, all the riders, more than ever.

“To have the chance to sit with all the riders in Phillip Island, to have the chance to sit here with our team managers, today with Mr. Ezpeleta, it's great, it's great, trust me.”

item.title: Mir explains the vision issues behind his long MotoGP absence
item.description: Joan Mir has revealed that vision problems and associated chronic fatigue were behind his absence from MotoGP race action for the past six weeks
item.dc:creator: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded:
Joan Mir has revealed that vision problems and associated chronic fatigue were behind his absence from MotoGP race action for the past six weeks.

But now with a full treatment plan completed and weeks of rest at home, he feels ready to return at 100% for this weekend's Malaysian Grand Prix at Sepang.

Mir withdrew from San Marino GP in mid-September following complaints of fatigue and, following adverse blood tests in the days after, has been on the long term sick list since, missing 44 days from the paddock and races in Austria, Japan, Indonesia, and Australia.

With little information on his condition over the past weeks, there has been plenty of paddock speculation about what exactly the 2020 world champion was suffering from, with vision issues one of the theories raised - something he explained on his return to the paddock without going into too much detail.

"I'm so happy to be back," he replied when asked by The Race about his condition. "As you can imagine. It's been a period that I simply needed to stop, because I had some vision problems that at the beginning we didn't really know what was happening.

"Related to this was the tiredness, but quite extreme. It was a process that was getting worse in the last races I did, in the first part of the season. I was forced to stop. I started treatment with [MotoGP medical director] Doctor Charte, and we could understand a little bit the problem.

"I think the cause was related to one problem I had in the past with the vision, and with the stress of the races it was getting worse. The tiredness was related to this thing, but until the moment where we understood this thing, we made a lot of tests."

Prior to his long-term absence from the paddock, it's not exactly been an easy season for Mir in his final stint as a Honda racer, crashing out of nine of his 14 full distance MotoGP races this season so far.

But, now armed with the understanding of the condition his body was in throughout the season, he also says that he's now able to start putting together some of the pieces that explain his year as well as returning to action at his maximum.

"Now I have a lot of answers about the things that happened," he explained. "In the end, I will keep it for me, for my future, but I think it will be something very important for the future.

"Tomorrow I will tell you [if I am at 100%], because it's not the same to go with the training bike, with the speed you go there and the speed you go here. It's different. But how I feel is a lot better than before, and I expect that I will feel good."

Marini returns too

The works Honda team was forced to withdraw entirely from last week's Phillip Island event as it wasn't running Mir's bike due to injuries to previous stand-ins Taka Nakagami and Aleix Espargaro and then lost team-mate Luca Marini to illness too after just two practice laps.

Marini is also fit to return this weekend, so Honda is back to full strength. His condition was described last weekend as a virus, and he explained the unusual symptoms on Thursday at Sepang.

"It was pretty strange," said Marini, "something I have never felt before. Really zero strength, zero power, but also a lot of problems to move my hands, my fingers, and my feet. Like arthritis.

"It was even difficult to write a message with the phone, something that I've never had before.

"After the first laps in Phillip Island I understood that it was a stupid thing to try and race there.

"Yesterday was the first day that I started to feel OK, and today I made another step, so I'm pretty sure that here I can compete more or less as normal. Obviously I will not be at 100% without training, without jumping on the bike, but just to be on the bike will be a pleasure."

item.title: Martin cleared to ride with broken wrist as he tries to stay in title hunt
item.description: Jorge Martin will ride in Sepang practice but his chances of making the race sound slim at best
item.dc:creator: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded:
Jorge Martin has been passed fit to ride in first practice at the Malaysian Grand Prix after breaking his wrist last Saturday but his chances of making the race and staying in the MotoGP title fight sound slim at best.

Once follow-up scans on Sunday revealed that the injury from his fall in the Phillip Island sprint race was not as severe or complex as first feared, Martin stayed in the region with the clear intention of trying to race at Sepang, rather than returning home to Spain for treatment.

He was passed fit to ride in Sepang FP1 on Thursday morning and will be checked again by the MotoGP medical team after that session.

But while declaring himself neither optimistic nor pessimistic about his situation, Martin's admissions that he cannot brush his teeth with his injured right side and that he would definitely not be trying to race on if he wasn't in the title fight do not bode well.

"I feel good. For sure, I could be worse, I could be better," the Aprilia rider replied when asked about his condition by The Race.

"Now we achieved the first step, that is to try to ride and then let's see my condition, let's see my feeling and then we will decide what to do next, if I continue with the GP or not.

"The only thing I know is that my wrist is broken. This is the only thing I know, that I will try to ride with a broken wrist, so for sure it will be really difficult, it will be really painful.

"I will try for sure because I'm in the title fight, because otherwise I will be in a house with a cast for one month.

"But the only thing I can do is to try, at least to try. That's why I'm here and the options I don't really know, I need to understand, I need to go on track. Let's see how much it's a limitation for the riding style.

"It's the right hand, which is the brake and the throttle. It's a right-corner circuit. So overall, it doesn't look great, but let's see tomorrow.

"I still cannot brush my teeth [with the right hand], I do it with the left hand, so I cannot do almost anything, but maybe I can ride. 

"I'm not really optimistic, not too pessimistic, because after five days I'm here and I can ride. So it's already, I think, crazy.

"I did all the therapies I could during this week to try to be in the best possible condition here, and now let's see how far I can go. 

"I'm just thinking of trying to ride. I don't think about the championship, I don't think about Sunday or Saturday, I think about tomorrow, let's try to ride, then I will move forward with my next step.

"At the moment I don't really feel really confident to race, but everything can happen, and for sure I felt a lot of improvement during the days.

"So maybe I don't feel well tomorrow, but maybe on Saturday I feel better. The process of the bone, it is what it is."

The crash while battling title rival and eventual race victor Marc Marquez last weekend left Martin 10 points behind in the championship, but the cancellation of the Australian GP itself removed a chance for Marquez to pull further clear.

Martin's description of his limitations on Thursday suggests that gap will only grow this weekend, even if he somehow makes it as far as competing in the race.

Aprilia's other rider in doubt

Like Martin, Trackhouse Aprilia rider Raul Fernandez was cleared to ride in Sepang FP1 during a medical check on Thursday.

But Fernandez sounds even less likely to try to race, as he wants to avoid further damage to the finger injury sustained in Indonesia that has already caused him to retire from the Phillip Island sprint.

Though Fernandez raced to a podium in the Indonesian GP the day after getting hurt in the sprint start crash, his experience in Australia has made him wary of exacerbating the problem and completely compromising the end of his season.

"I feel worse than in Australia," Fernandez admitted on Thursday.

"The fracture is still not recovered, to be honest. I want to try, I am here and for sure I will jump on the bike and we will see how the finger is, but to be honest it is not necessary to take too many risks, I need to recover it.

It is a very important finger for me, it is the one that I am using normally to brake. Also now it's in a moment that it is coming to recovery, so if I crash again I will start from zero, so I don't want to do a stupid thing."

item.title: Australian GP 2026 MotoGP rider rankings
item.description: Yes, the 2026 Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island didn't quite happen. But we've still found a way to grade an extremely incomplete weekend
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
Yes, before you say it, you're right - the 2026 Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island didn't quite happen. We are grading an extremely incomplete weekend.

But a MotoGP race did happen at Phillip Island and was potentially, unfortunately, the most pivotal MotoGP race of the year in terms of the title fight. It was also a really good one, and clearly treated as a proper contest by the participants.

Because of this, and the relevant preceding context of the weekend's 1,276 MotoGP laps before the sprint, here is our ranking of the premier-class performers at Phillip Island.

Qualifying: 1st Sprint: 1st

When it comes to riders taking on Marc Marquez in a title fight, I think the myth does almost as much work as the man. His rivals cannot help but feel the inevitability with which his triumphs are spoken of, and they certainly cannot ignore his track record.

But you need some myth-making to keep the myth at its most potent. And Marquez's performance on Saturday morning was exactly that - a ritual humiliation of the rest of the grid that sent a message of 'you really should beat me in the dry, because you can't live with me in the wet'.

The lap that he crashed on at the start of Q2 began with a 24.394s first sector. Over the rest of Q2, only Johann Zarco even got within a tenth of that. Marquez wasn't fighting Zarco, or his brother, or Jack Miller - he was fighting the ground.

The more conventional sprint conditions made him sweat a bit more, but he was relentless in keeping the pressure on Martin - which turned a likely defeat into a pivotal victory.

Admittedly, brother Alex went easy on him, and Fabio Di Giannantonio may have been quicker, too. But I don't actually believe that Marc was ever losing that race once Martin went down - regardless of familiar or manufacturer ties.

Qualifying: 5th Sprint: 7th

If this wasn't the best Miller has looked as a MotoGP rider at Phillip Island, it wasn't too far off at all.

He was the quickest Yamaha rider in every session that ran, and quickest by a lot in wet/mixed conditions, living up to his reputation.

A fifth-to-eighth in the sprint (then eighth-to-seventh thanks to Ai Ogura's post-race penalty) was widely recognised as valiant given the Yamaha's lack of performance on the main straight. "Poor guy was standing still" was how Brad Binder described it.

Qualifying: 2nd Sprint: 2nd

A high-quality weekend from a rider who I've never really associated with Phillip Island success - despite track characteristics that should suggest a degree of favourability.

While Marc made the rest of the grid look like 'little brothers', Alex proved the most credible combatant, and perhaps could have won the sprint had he avoided the early tussle with Acosta.

Once it was just down to him and Marc, though late in the race, Alex pretty clearly settled for second. I can't say I blame him in this particular situation.

Qualifying: 7th Sprint: 5th

The performance picture within the KTM ranks across the various conditions of this curtailed weekend is a little murky, but there's little question Acosta got the most out of the RC16 - despite finding the bike insufficiently stable.

He adopted a 'charge, then defend' strategy for the sprint, with a very impressive first run through the Southern Loop corner and then ultimately no real hope of beating the bikes ahead but enough pace to coast comfortably to an impressive top-five.

Qualifying: 3rd Sprint: DNF

The standout of a diminished Honda roster - by a lot in the wet, by a negligible/unclear margin in the dry.

There's a lot to be said for Zarco's sheer dependability when it comes to a damp track, and his medium front gamble in the sprint (nobody else ran it) looked to be paying off in the early laps of the contest.

We'll never know what the downside would have been later in the race because an apparent electronics problem removed him from the contest.

Qualifying: 14th Sprint: 9th

You should know that the Phillip Island round of this past World Superbike season was Lecuona's worst - though much more through an extremely compromised pre-season and sped-up bike adaptation than any kind of track-specific struggles.

Here, save for a couple of crashes, he was super-good again as a stand-in for Fermin Aldeguer. He is clearly faster than one Ducati regular (Franco Morbidelli), maybe faster than another (Pecco Bagnaia) and faster than his race results suggest, given a certain MotoGP-rustiness does come out in the early laps of races.

This is now three weekends of extremely credible MotoGP production from Lecuona on short notice. I didn't believe it before - but I am legitimately starting to wonder whether Lecuona, who will again deputise for Aldeguer at Sepang, could be more in this paddock in the future than just a cameo hero.

Qualifying: 8th Sprint: 3rd

Di Giannantonio is very good at Phillip Island - but dry Phillip Island rather than wet Phillip Island, which meant that his sprint ride was always going to have to make up for a suboptimal qualifying.

He was very lucky, in hindsight, to just sneak into Q2 on Friday - then unlucky to encounter Ai Ogura-shaped traffic on what he believed would've been a much better qualifying lap (by two-three tenths) than what he ended up with.

His ride in the sprint from lap two was unimpeachable. Lap one was pretty-pretty bad.

Qualifying: 9th Sprint: 4th

Bezzecchi was very lucky to get away relatively scot-free with a very clumsy crash into Alex Marquez in Friday practice.

He bounced back from that to end the day quickest, and generally looked through the weekend's dry-weather portions like the favourite to win.

Unfortunately for him, Q2 wasn't one of those dry-weather portions, and after a credible performance with more water on track in the preceding practice, he surprisingly struggled in qualifying.

Losing more ground at the start in the sprint (he got boxed in behind Raul Fernandez's still "low" bike, so lost out to Diogo Moreira and Enea Bastianini) meant it was only ever going to be a salvage job, despite his searing pace.

Qualifying: 10th Sprint: 8th

Another weekend of solid proof that the second 2027 factory Honda seat - now officially assigned to Moreira - is in good hands.

On Friday morning, at first MotoGP contact with the track, he had found the Honda "impossible to ride", but it was quickly dialled in and served him well over the rest of the weekend, enabling him to pick up a couple of consolation points for LCR after Zarco's misfortune.

Qualifying: 13th Sprint: 6th

More competitive than usual as of late - though, like his peers, limited by how the bike behaved in the wind.

A big smoky engine failure to start things on Friday didn't help, but Binder did a solid job in Q1 and made the most of the start to score a good result in the sole race.

Qualifying: 6th Sprint: DNF

Honestly very impressive for as long as his battered right hand allowed him to be.

Still braking with the middle finger rather than the recovering index finger, Fernandez showed a speed befitting of the defending Australian GP winner (which I guess he still is!) on Friday, and even in the less favourable conditions of Saturday morning.

Inflammation around the fracture meant he had to bail out on the sprint, and Sepang seems in a bit of doubt.

Qualifying: 19th Sprint: 10th

This certainly wasn't one of the better Quartararo weekends - he struggled for front feeling even in the dry, and didn't get anything out of qualifying despite seemingly having the right strategy.

A 10th place from the sole race of the weekend was a solid return, though primarily a consequence of other riders' misfortune and a more aggressive start than some of his Yamaha peers managed.

Qualifying: 18th Sprint: 12th

Rins outqualified Quartararo for just the second time this year - by three tenths, too - but just didn't do enough in the dry to rank ahead of his team-mate.

Last after the opening lap, he made impressive progress through some stragglers before running out of options behind the KTM of Enea Bastianini.

Qualifying: 4th Sprint: DNF

A disastrous crash that I have to judge harshly yet I struggle to - because I think Martin saw the same thing that I did, i.e. the spectre of a 10-second Marc Marquez victory in the rain on Sunday at a track which Aprilia had the dry-weather bike to dominate at.

He had assembled a very impressive weekend through practice and qualifying, and through the opening lap of the sprint, but looked ragged and desperate in his attempts to deal with Marc - and so lost the bike, the race and potentially the championship.

I hope he recovers very swiftly and gets an unlikely second chance of taking the fight to his relentless Ducati rival.

Qualifying: 11th Sprint: 11th

Bastianini doesn't like to deal with any kind of wind on the RC16, so had approached Phillip Island with some trepidation - but vastly overperformed expectations on Friday by waltzing to a Q2 spot.

His bike's electronics set-up proved unfit for purpose in the wet (and he didn't get the chance to verify the fix on Sunday), and the sprint pace was mildly disappointing despite a lively start.

Qualifying: 12th Sprint: 13th

The wet-weather limitations feel increasingly existential for Ogura in MotoGP right now - there is no doubt he is a productive rider, but he does not want to carry a glaring weakness through the years. As he himself admitted at Phillip Island: "I have to plan something! I cannot continue like this for all my career."

Despite his lack of affinity for the circuit, all the dry-weather bits were totally fine. But he would've qualified a distant last if not for the Friday Q1/Q2 split.

He rode a reasonable sprint but hadn't made quite enough progress in the early going, and then had the accrued points thrown away for a tyre pressure breach, rendering the weekend a waste.

Qualifying: 15th Sprint: DNF

Still unfortunately just not fit to ride a MotoGP bike at the level of his ability - particularly at a punishing track like Phillip Island.

Things looked slightly better in the rain, which makes sense, but overall it's very sad and frustrating, and the only hope now is that shedding the pressures of a full-time schedule will enable Vinales to look like himself again at some point down the line, hopefully in a Ducati test role.

Qualifying: 17th Sprint: 15th

Out of practice with the 1,000cc bike and Michelin rubber, Fernandez struggled for pace in the dry - his fastest lap in the sprint nearly two seconds worse than his peers managed, and his predicament such that he quickly lost touch with the pack and couldn't maintain sufficient front tyre pressure to avoid a (meaningless) post-race penalty.

A minor positive, though, is a commendable performance in the wet qualifying, to beat both Quartararo and Rins.

Qualifying: 16th Sprint: DNF

The motivation to dig out any extra meaning from these late-season Pecco Bagnaia weekends is, to put it mildly, waning. He's tired of the bike, the bike seems tired of him, and the remaining sessions are all busywork.

He was very poor here - he "didn't do a great lap" on Friday but probably just didn't quite have the performance for Q2 anyway, then underwhelmed in the Saturday morning rain. He did feel a shot at passage through Q1 was thrown away by the decision to go for a single extended wet medium rear run - but I am honestly not convinced he could have found enough laptime.

He was unusually cagey on the "problem" - seemingly not a mechanical problem - that took him out of the sprint, which was already by then a total write-off.

Qualifying: 20th Sprint: 14th

A dreadful low point in a season bursting at the seams with them. It would be better for everyone involved if VR46 sent him home on a get-right mission ahead of his World Superbike switch, and brought in Lecuona to do the remaining rounds.

This might sound harsh, and it is harsh, but nothing at all is working for Morbidelli. He had clearly hoped, not without reason, that a wet-weather curveball would allow him to compensate for his total mismatch with the Ducati GP25 - but even in the wet, this normally assured rain rider looked totally lost.

"Now I seem to not extract anything from this '25 package" was his blunt admission.

item.title: MotoGP's final Phillip Island race cancelled, replaced with parade lap
item.description: The 2026 Australian Grand Prix MotoGP race at Phillip Island has been cancelled due to adverse weather conditions
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Australian Grand Prix MotoGP race at Phillip Island has been cancelled due to adverse weather conditions.

"Poor visibility affecting the operation of the medical helicopter" meant the day's planned track action in any of the three classes of grand prix racing never got under way - as there was never a sufficient break in the weather to even attempt racing.

MotoGP first cancelled the Moto3 race, then the Moto2 race, then finally called off the premier-class event at 3.35pm local time - having accepted that the hope to get the race started at 4.30pm was in vain.

In lieu of the race, MotoGP riders "will do a lap behind the safety car and stop on the main straight to greet the fans".

This will function as a "farewell lap" to the Phillip Island venue, which will be replaced as the host of the Australian GP next year by the street track in Adelaide.

Race organisers have confirmed that they are "working with our ticketing partners to facilitate the process for full refunds for Sunday ticketholders and partial refunds for multi-day ticketholders".

"To every fan who came to Phillip Island today, despite the conditions, thank you. Your support is a powerful reminder of the love for MotoGP and the special place Phillip Island holds in Australian motorsport," they said in a statement.

"While this is not the way anyone wanted MotoGP's time at Phillip Island to conclude, it does not diminish the incredible legacy of this event. We thank the fans, riders, teams, officials, volunteers, partners and the Phillip Island community who have made it so special over so many years."

The premier class, MotoGP, at least exits Phillip Island having contested a sprint race in the dry. Moto3 and Moto2 fields will leave without having raced, after logging a respective 1446 laps and 1500 laps across practice and qualifying on the two previous days.

Sunday had long been anticipated to offer the worst of the weather this weekend - but MotoGP did not pursue a repeat of its 2023 strategy, when it successfully ran the full-distance grand prix on Saturday and then scheduled the sprint on Sunday (and subsequently cancelled it).

Championship leader Marc Marquez leaves Phillip Island with a 10-point cushion over Jorge Martin with a scheduled four rounds left (as question marks remain over the Qatar Grand Prix).

The Sunday cancellation is a massive reprieve for the injured Martin, who it is thought will attempt to compete next weekend at Sepang.

item.title: Martin injury update hints at early racing return bid
item.description: Injured title contender Jorge Martin may be targeting a sooner than expected return to race action
item.dc:creator: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded:
MotoGP championship contender Jorge Martin may be targeting a sooner than expected return to race action after the Phillip Island injury that seemed to have ended his title shot.

Martin’s Aprilia team announced on Sunday morning that Martin will remain in Australia this week despite breaking his arm on Saturday during the sprint race.

That potentially opens the door for an attempted return at Sepang in one week’s time.

Initial reports from the team on Saturday afternoon suggested that Martin had broken both the radius and ulna in his right arm, but said that he would first travel to hospital in Melbourne (two hours away from the Phillip Island track) for further assessment.

That assessment turned out to be good news, with a suspected fracture of his ulna (the smaller bone in the lower arm) ruled out.

“Jorge Martin underwent a CT scan to assess his condition following yesterday’s injury. The only confirmed injury is a non-displaced fracture of the distal radius,” said Aprilia’s statement.

“Consequently, the rider will not be returning to Spain and will undergo the necessary treatment over the coming days.”

With MotoGP travelling directly from Australia to Malaysia for the next of its back-to-back races at Sepang, the news that Martin will not go back home but will instead remain in the region very much opens the door for an attempt to return next weekend.

His crash out of Saturday’s sprint and Marc Marquez’s subsequent victory has tipped the championship lead clearly in favour of the Ducati rider for the first time this year, turning Martin’s slender two-point lead into a 10-point breathing space for Marquez.

However, with heavy rain and reduced visibility throwing Sunday’s main event (and its potential 25 points) at Phillip Island into doubt, it could be a case of extenuating circumstances helping Martin limit the damage, making a prospective return at Sepang slightly more palatable.

item.title: Fernandez becomes sixth rider sidelined from Australian GP
item.description: Defending Australian Grand Prix winner Raul Fernandez has been named as the sixth full-time MotoGP rider sidelined from this year’s Phillip Island race
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
Defending Australian Grand Prix winner Raul Fernandez has been named as the sixth full-time MotoGP rider sidelined from this year’s Phillip Island race.

Fernandez joins Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini Ducati), Joan Mir (Honda), Luca Marini (Honda), Toprak Razgatlioglu (Pramac Yamaha) and Jorge Martin (Aprilia) as an absentee from Sunday’s event.

Aldeguer, Mir and Razgatlioglu are missing the weekend due to various injury and health reasons and an ill Marini had to throw in the towel after two laps in practice, while Martin got injured in the sprint.

Fernandez, meanwhile, is nursing an injury from Mandalika - where he had to use a different braking technique in the grand prix race after sustaining a right index finger fracture in the sprint start crash  - and was forced to drop out of the Australian GP sprint by his physical condition.

His Trackhouse team has now confirmed that his Phillip Island weekend is over, and that he is in doubt for next weekend's round at Sepang, which offers no shortage of braking challenges.

"After the race, Fernandez went straight to a medical assessment with the MotoGP medical director [Dr Angel Charte] and it was found that while the finger fracture is stable, there is inflammation of the soft tissue around the fracture," Trackhouse explained.

Fernandez will have a medical assessment on Thursday at Sepang so is at least set to attend the weekend.

His absence brings the grand prix field down to 18 bikes, as only two of the six absentees are being covered by stand-ins.

Gresini has Iker Lecuona on Aldeguer’s Ducati and Augusto Fernandez will complete the season on Razgatlioglu’s Pramac Yamaha.

But while Fernandez, Martin and Marini’s withdrawals all happened during Saturday, Honda was already unable to cover for Mir because its test riders Taka Nakagami and Aleix Espargaro are also injured. So Marini dropping out as well leaves its works team with no bikes on the grid.

item.title: Arm injury effectively ends Martin's MotoGP title chance
item.description: Arm fracture from his Phillip Island sprint crash sidelines Jorge Martin and all but ends his title bid
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
Jorge Martin and his Aprilia MotoGP team have suffered a huge blow in the 2026 title race, with at least one fracture discovered after his crash in the Phillip Island sprint.

Martin exited the sprint race at the fast Hayshed corner (Turn 8) after a multi-lap lead battle with title rival Marc Marquez.

He rolled violently through the gravel and was taken to the medical centre on a stretcher, before emerging from it with his right arm in a cast.

Aprilia subsequently revealed that Martin has fractured his right arm - and while he will still require further examinations to determine the full extent of the damage, he has been declared unfit for the remainder of the Phillip Island weekend.

According to Aprilia, a fracture to the right radial bone - one of the two primary bones in the forearm - has been definitively diagnosed. But there is also a suspected fracture to the other primary forearm bone, the ulna, "at the distal end" (which means towards the wrist rather than the elbow).

No recovery timeline has been outlined given the absence of a full diagnosis, but the injury makes it all but impossible for Martin to realistically remain in this title race.

He is 10 points behind Marquez in the standings and will miss Sunday's race, but the injury has also come at the start of a planned triple-header (covering also the Sepang race and the in-doubt Qatar race).

Martin had suffered two radial fractures already (both on the left arm) earlier in his grand prix career.

One came during the 2018 season in Moto3, forcing him to miss one race but with a quick enough recovery to enable him to win the title that year, while the other happened before the start of the 2025 season and (along with a spate of other injuries from the same crash) sidelined him for two rounds.

item.title: Marquez retakes MotoGP lead after epic duel and big Martin crash
item.description: Marc Marquez took a crucial victory in the Phillip Island sprint, as title rival Jorge Martin crashed out from their epic duel
item.dc:creator: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded:
Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez took a crucial victory in the sprint race at Phillip Island, as title rival Jorge Martin crashed out from their epic duel.

It was the dry sprint Aprilia would have hoped for given Marquez's supremacy in the wet in qualifying earlier today - but instead it suffered a heavy title blow, and Martin faces fitness concerns after being stretchered off from the site of his crash.

Martin had gone fourth-to-second at the start, though had to fight off a counter-attack from Alex Marquez during the second lap as a five-bike lead group established itself.

But as Martin challenged Marc Marquez out front, a lunge on Alex by Pedro Acosta allowed the lead duo breathing room - and they spent the next handful of laps in a back-and-forth squabble for the lead.

Martin would repeatedly take first and then give it up through errors - going wide at the Miller corner, then at the Southern Loop - or to Marc counter-attacks.

Finally, with Alex bearing down on them again after fighting off Acosta, it proved one counter-attack too many for Martin - who crashed at speed coming through Hayshed and rolled violently in the gravel.

He didn't immediately look in obvious strife in the aftermath of the crash, but then was put on a stretcher and taken to the medical centre for checks.

Marc Marquez controlled the race from there, with no real challenge forthcoming from Alex, and now heads Martin by 10 points in the standings.

Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati) and Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) worked their way through the order, having sat seventh and 10th after the start, and just ran out of laps to challenge for second place.

Bezzecchi now trails Marc Marquez by 50 points in the standings.

Acosta, Ai Ogura, Brad Binder, home hero Jack Miller and 'lone Honda standing' Diogo Moreira initially made up the points.

But Ogura faced an investigation for a potential tyre pressure infringement, and when his penalty was applied Gresini Ducati stand-in Iker Lecuona picked up a point.

Martin was the only rider to crash out - but there were four other retirements in Raul Fernandez (seemingly fitness-related), Maverick Vinales, Pecco Bagnaia and Johann Zarco, the latter bowing out due to an apparent mechanical issue while in the top five.

item.title: Marquez falls on his way to staggering Phillip Island MotoGP pole
item.description: Marc Marquez took pole for MotoGP's Australian GP by a staggering 1.5 seconds at a wet Phillip Island, despite crashing on his first Q2 lap
item.dc:creator: Matt Beer
item.content:encoded:
Marc Marquez took pole for MotoGP's Australian Grand Prix by a staggering 1.5 seconds at a wet Phillip Island, despite crashing on his first Q2 lap.

With fresh rain falling as Q2 began, that low-side crash into the Miller corner looked like it might leave Marquez a disastrous 12th on the grid.

But he managed to remount his Ducati, the rain eased again, and with the track to himself for his next lap Marquez jumped to pole.

Rain ace Johann Zarco had been fastest at first and did take provisional pole back from Marquez for a while on the next runs.

Then Marquez utterly blew everyone else away on the last laps of the session though, putting in a 1m34.203s that was an astonishing 1.494s faster than the eventual second-place rider, his brother Alex on the Gresini Ducati.

Zarco kept his LCR Honda on the front row in third.

Marquez's title rival Jorge Martin never looked like he had pole pace in the damp but making it back up to fourth on the grid with his last lap counts as a very good save considering Marquez's pace.

Martin's long-shot championship contender Aprilia team-mate Marco Bezzecchi didn't manage that - he starts only ninth for the weekend's two races.

Home hero Jack Miller was fastest in Q1 and briefly had a provisional front row in Q2 before ending up a still heartwarming fifth for Pramac Yamaha.

Performances varied in the conditions, with Marquez's astonishing pole at one end of the field in stark contrast to how far off the pace tail end pair Fabio Quartararo and Franco Morbidelli were in 19th and 20th on the reduced grid that will lack any factory Hondas following the unwell Luca Marini's withdrawal.

item.title: Works Honda team runs out of riders for Australian GP
item.description: The factory Honda MotoGP team will play no further part in the Australian Grand Prix weekend having effectively run out of riders
item.dc:creator: Matt Beer
item.content:encoded:
The factory Honda MotoGP team will play no further part in the Australian Grand Prix weekend having effectively run out of riders.

Luca Marini was already representing the team solo at Phillip Island but was unwell on Friday and only completed two slow practice laps.

Honda then announced just before Saturday track action started that Marini would not be able to compete this weekend after being declared unfit by MotoGP medical director Dr Angel Charte.

"For the past week, Luca Marini has been suffering from a viral condition and a high fever for three to four days," said Dr Charte.

"For the last 48 to 72 hours, he has been suffering from muscle weakness caused by the virus, affecting both his upper and lower body.

"During the last examination, conducted on Saturday morning, he presented with the same symptoms and was declared unfit."

Marini's team-mate Joan Mir has been absent since mid-September due to an illness that his medical team were struggling to fully diagnose.

There have been suggestions in the paddock this weekend that Mir might be ready to try to return to MotoGP at next week's Malaysian GP - where Marini will also be assessed again.

Though Honda was also in this situation as recently as the September 2024 Misano event, where both Mir and Marini also pulled out with illnesses, the situation is made more bizarre this time by the lack of stand-in options as its two main test riders are both injured.

Taka Nakagami impressed as Mir's Austrian GP replacement but then broke his collarbone in a crash on his very first lap of the following event in Japan.

Aleix Espargaro got the next call-up - with the Indonesian GP his first MotoGP appearance since injuring his back in a test crash in April - but Espargaro withdrew mid-weekend and has since headed for arm pump surgery.

Former LCR rider Somkiat Chantra - now part of Honda's factory World Superbike squad - was also used as Mir's stand-in for Motegi, where Nakagami's aborted entry was as an already-planned wildcard - but Honda has indicated it is keeping him focused on Superbike testing this week.

item.title: Grid drops? New MotoGP sanctions for missing PR events revealed
item.description: MotoGP riders can now face sporting sanctions for missing PR activities during race weekends, according to new rules issued in secret to teams at this weekend’s Australian Grand Prix
item.dc:creator: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded:
MotoGP riders can now face sporting sanctions for missing PR activities during race weekends, according to new rules issued in secret to teams at this weekend’s Australian Grand Prix.

Riders will face time suspended from practice sessions and even grid penalties should they fail to turn up to mandated promotional events during race weekends.

The rules were issued to teams in a confidential email sent by the International Race Team Association on Friday and seen by The Race, and presumably comes as a reaction to reigning world champion Marc Marquez refusing to participate in a Sunday morning go-kart race at the Japanese Grand Prix earlier this month.

The new sanctions are to ensure that the championship’s "commitments made to fans, commercial partners and event organisers are respected", and come, according to the email, after "repeated instances of non-compliance have made it necessary to introduce a clear and transparent escalation process".

They will mean that on the first instance of missing the Thursday press conference, pre-race promotional activities, Sunday morning riders’ parade, or the mandatory 10-minute attendance at autograph sessions or the Hero Walk event, riders will be issued with an official warning.

On the second offence, they will be fined €5,000. That rises to €10,000 for a third offence and €15,000 for a fourth offence, as well as being escalated to the FIM MotoGP Stewards - a body whose previous role was only to issue sporting sanctions on track - for an official warning.

A fifth offence will then see riders docked time from a practice session - while a sixth offence will see Simon Crafar’s stewarding team hand out a grid penalty.

Exceptions will be made for riders with "injury or the requirement for medical attention", as well as those who have prior PR commitments with their teams - but the document seen by The Race stresses that late arrival and leaving early from events will be treated as a failure to attend.

The document also stresses that the new approach "is consistent with professional sport more broadly, where participation in official media, promotional and fan engagement activities form part of an athlete's responsibilities and clear processes exist to address repeated non-compliance".

Attendance at scheduled media appearances outside of Thursday’s press conference is not included in the list of events for which riders can be punished.

The introduction of sporting sanctions comes after Marquez refused to participate in the Sunday morning activity at Motegi, initially sending a stunt double before being found out and reprimanded by the series’ bosses.

Speaking afterwards, Marquez stressed that while he understands the importance of growing the sport, something that has come under increased focus thanks to new owners Liberty Media, he believes that racing motorcycles must remain his primary and overriding focus.

“There is a bit of a line,” he stressed. “Obviously I understand the show, but we are fighting for the championship, we’re not here to mess around or go around in kart races.

“After the warm-up I needed ice [on the injured right shoulder], and someone came out and said it would be cool to send a doppelganger, and we did it.

“They told me off, but at this moment you have to be selfish and perform at your maximum when it matters, which is in the races.”

Rule changes for 2027 announced earlier this month will see Sunday morning’s warm-up session scrapped to make more time for promotional activities like the Japanese go-kart race. At this weekend’s Phillip Island event, riders are set to head out on track in electric mini jeeps for the fan parade.
